content_html:
Hotel Manager Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A hotel manager resume has a harder job than most operations resumes. Owners want revenue and profit. Brands want standards compliance and guest scores. Management companies want a leader who can run a whole property without daily supervision. One generic resume cannot answer all three.

This guide gives you a full annotated example for a general manager of a mid-size hotel, a section-by-section breakdown, and the mistakes that cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works: what you ran, at what scale, and with what result.

Quick answer: A hotel manager resume should include a summary naming the property size and type you ran; an operations block with rooms, team size, and annual revenue; experience bullets pairing each duty with an occupancy, revenue, or guest-satisfaction result, such as RevPAR growth; and keywords like Opera PMS, revenue management, and guest recovery, spelled as postings spell them.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with scope — rooms, team size, and annual revenue — in the summary and in its own block.
  • Every experience bullet pairs a duty with a count: occupancy, RevPAR, or guest scores.
  • Show both sides: revenue growth for the owner and guest experience for the brand.
  • Name the systems you can run on day one: Opera PMS and channel managers.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so applicant tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Hotel Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to a hotel owner and you will not hear “passionate hospitality professional.” You will hear:

  • Scope, stated plainly. Rooms, team size, annual revenue, and whether you owned the profit-and-loss statement. A 40-room boutique and a 400-room hotel are different jobs.
  • Revenue proof. Occupancy, average daily rate, RevPAR, and gross operating profit, with the before and after. Owners hire managers who move numbers, not managers who describe duties.
  • Guest-experience numbers, not guest-experience adjectives. Review scores, Net Promoter Score, complaint resolution times, repeat-guest rates. Prove it with counts.
  • Team leadership at scale. Hiring, training, scheduling, and retention across departments that never sleep. A manager who kept a 45-person team staffed through a peak season is a safer hire than one who only ran a shift.
  • Standards and safety discipline. Brand audits passed, health and safety inspections cleared, food-safety compliance, incident handling. One failed audit can cost a property its flag.

If your resume reads like a duties list — all responsibilities, no outcomes — it will lose to one that reads like an operating record.

Hotel Manager Resume Example (Annotated)

Below is a complete example for a general manager of a 180-room hotel. It’s fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern hiring managers respond to: what you ran, the scale, and the result.

MARCUS THOMPSON
Atlanta, GA · (404) 555-0147 · marcus.thompson@email.com

SUMMARY
Hotel manager with 9 years across full-service and boutique properties, including 4 years as general manager of a 180-room hotel. Grew occupancy from 68% to 82% and RevPAR 18% in two years; hold a 4.8 out of 5 guest-satisfaction score across 3,200+ reviews. Lead a 45-person team on a $6.2M annual budget; CHA-certified.

PROPERTY SCOPE & CERTIFICATIONS
180-room full-service hotel · 45-person team · $6.2M annual revenue · Certified Hotel Administrator (CHA) · Food safety certification, current · First aid & CPR, current · B.S., Hospitality Management, Georgia State University, 2016

SKILLS
Revenue management · Opera PMS · Guest recovery · Front office operations · Housekeeping management · Food and beverage operations · Events and banquets · Budgeting and P&L · Staff training · Brand standards · Channel management · Dynamic pricing · Health and safety compliance · Vendor negotiation

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

General Manager — The Meridian Hotel, Atlanta, GA | 2021–Present

  • Run a 180-room full-service hotel with a 45-person team on a $6.2M annual budget, owning the full profit-and-loss statement and the owner relationship
  • Grew occupancy from 68% to 82% and RevPAR 18% in two years through dynamic pricing, a direct-booking push, and a rebuilt corporate rate program
  • Hold a 4.8 out of 5 guest-satisfaction score across 3,200+ reviews, up from 4.3, by rebuilding the guest-recovery process so every complaint gets a same-day response
  • Cut housekeeping cost per occupied room 12% by re-sequencing shifts and renegotiating the linen contract
  • Grew events revenue 22% by repackaging the ballroom for midweek corporate groups and adding a wedding-showcase weekend

Assistant General Manager — The Meridian Hotel, Atlanta, GA | 2019–2021

  • Ran daily operations across front office, housekeeping, and food and beverage, covering the general manager during 40+ absence days with no service failures
  • Led the front office team of 14, cutting average check-in time from 6 minutes to under 3 and lifting upsell revenue 15%
  • Introduced a weekly revenue meeting that aligned sales, front office, and housekeeping on one occupancy forecast, ending double-booked event space
  • Passed two brand quality audits with scores above 90%, clearing every corrective action within 30 days

Front Office Manager — Harborview Inn, Savannah, GA | 2017–2019

  • Managed front desk operations for a 90-room boutique hotel, scheduling a team of 8
  • Raised the property’s review score from 4.1 to 4.6 by training the team on a five-minute guest-recovery standard
  • Handled group arrivals for 12 weddings and conferences a year from a single run sheet

EDUCATION
B.S., Hospitality Management — Georgia State University, 2016

Why it works: the summary leads with scope and the two numbers owners check — occupancy with RevPAR growth, and the guest-satisfaction score. Every bullet pairs a duty with a count, and the climb from front office manager to general manager shows the whole progression.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: scope first, then revenue and guest scores

“180-room hotel,” “$6.2M annual budget,” “occupancy from 68% to 82%,” “4.8 out of 5” — the scope answers the sizing question; the revenue pair answers the competence question. If you have never owned a P&L, say so plainly and lead with the operation you did run.

Experience: results, not responsibilities

“Managed the front office” is a responsibility; “cut average check-in time from 6 minutes to under 3 and lifted upsell revenue 15%” is proof of management. The strongest bullets show a number that moved because of a decision you made.

Scope: rooms, team, and budget, in one block

List the property size, the team, the annual revenue, and every current certification. Hiring managers size the job from this block before reading experience.

Hotel Manager Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting’s language exactly: “revenue management” vs “yield management” matters:

  • Revenue: revenue management, RevPAR, ADR, occupancy, dynamic pricing, channel management, direct bookings, corporate rates, forecasting
  • Operations: front office, housekeeping, food and beverage, events and banquets, maintenance coordination, inventory, vendor negotiation
  • Guest experience: guest recovery, guest satisfaction, Net Promoter Score, review management, concierge, loyalty programs
  • Systems: Opera PMS, channel managers, property management systems, point of sale, housekeeping software, revenue tools
  • Credentials: CHA, Certified Hotel Administrator, food safety certification, hospitality management degree, first aid

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Hotels screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. Start from a clean template in Cvyon's template gallery, or the role page for hotel managers. Note the difference from the office manager role: office managers run a business office, hotel managers run a whole property around the clock.

5 Mistakes That Cost Hotel Managers Interviews

  1. Hiding the scope. A resume that never states rooms, team size, or revenue forces the reader to guess. Put scope in the summary and in its own block.
  2. Listing duties instead of results. “Responsible for front office operations” is a job description; “cut check-in time from 6 minutes to under 3 and lifted upsell revenue 15%” is management. Lead with results.
  3. Claiming a certification you do not hold. “CHA” when you have never sat the exam is a misrepresentation brands verify. State it honestly: “CHA candidate” or “CHA exam scheduled.”
  4. No revenue numbers. Occupancy, ADR, RevPAR, gross operating profit — a resume without a revenue number reads as if revenue was never measured.
  5. One generic resume for boutique and branded hotels. Tailor the summary and first bullets to the property: guest experience and reviews for boutique, standards compliance and audit scores for branded.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in a hotel manager resume?

A summary naming the property size and type you ran; an operations block with rooms, team size, and annual revenue; experience bullets pairing each duty with an occupancy, revenue, or guest-satisfaction result, such as RevPAR growth; and keywords like Opera PMS and revenue management, spelled as postings spell them.

How do I show revenue impact on a hotel manager resume?

Lead with the numbers owners watch: occupancy, average daily rate, RevPAR, and gross operating profit. State the before and after wherever you can, for example occupancy from 68% to 82% or RevPAR up 18% in a year, and name the lever that moved it, such as dynamic pricing or direct-booking growth.

What is the difference between a hotel manager and a general manager on a resume?

In most properties the general manager owns the whole profit-and-loss statement and the owner relationship, while the hotel manager runs daily operations under them: front office, housekeeping, food and beverage, and maintenance. In smaller hotels the two titles often describe the same job. State the scope you actually held, with rooms, team, and budget.

How long should a hotel manager resume be?

One page for most hotel managers, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a career across genuinely different properties, such as a boutique hotel, a resort, and a branded hotel, that each need space; even then keep the scope and the strongest numbers on page one.

What certifications should a hotel manager list on a resume?

List the ones you actually hold: Certified Hotel Administrator (CHA), food-safety certification, and first-aid training are the common ones, plus a hospitality degree where you have it. Never claim a credential you do not hold; owners and brand auditors verify before the first interview.

Do I need hospitality experience to become a hotel manager?

Most rise through the property: front desk agent to supervisor to front office manager to assistant general manager. A hospitality degree helps, but a record of running a shift, a department, or a small property counts for more. Show the progression plainly, with the size of each operation.
